output.brief: The evidence does not support blaming the Admissions Office for the enrolment drop. Applications, admits and student quality all rose, so the applicant pool was not the problem. Yield fell only in the two scholarship tiers whose awards were cut (Dean's, from $14,000 to $9,000, and Merit, from $9,000 to $5,000), from about 45% to about 32%. Presidential awards were unchanged, and the no-award group barely moved (38.5% to 37.0%). Early-action students, whose decisions were not delayed, lost yield by almost the same amount as regular-decision students (7.4 points against 7.5). That points away from the portal delays as the main cause. The delays were real and may have cost a few individual students, such as the Westcombe case. I'm fairly confident, but I haven't checked competitor pricing, and the missing-transcript complaints are unverified. Next steps: don't replace the director. Take a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the net-revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Separately, set a turnaround target for regular decision and restore the reader capacity. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the missing-document claim is tested.
output.methodChoice: Collected X3 (yield by scholarship tier) and X15 (yield by round) to separate the scholarship, turnaround and general-demand explanations.
